accuracy.evidence: The three-part definition (repeated, intentional, imbalance of power) matches the Anti-Bullying Alliance definition and StopBullying.gov (aggressive behaviour, repetition, real or perceived power imbalance). The four forms (physical, verbal, social or relational, cyber) and the bystander duty to report to an adult match DfE Relationships Education guidance. No item calls a one-off accident or argument bullying.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips: every argument is bullying, only hitting counts so exclusion and name-calling are dismissed, telling makes it worse, hitting back or replying to cruel messages, deleting proof, and giving up after telling once. The adult text names the grown-up slip of 'just ignore it' when the child faces a power gap.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagbully combines a Mon-Fri week strip where the child marks the days a story names before judging once versus again and again, a power see-saw that tips with the bully's advantages and levels as helpers are added, and three card decks. flagprej is about group prejudice and the Equality Act; flagpal is about spotting a struggling friend. Shingle gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: Marking one day versus four or five days makes repetition visible before the verdict; the see-saw only levels once a grown-up, an upstander and kids saying 'Stop it!' join Ava, so the child sees why telling and standing together work. Each wrong drop names the reason, for example 'Laughing along joins in with the bully.'

predictions.evidence: Four locked predictions with tempting wrong options: a single shout-and-make-up is bullying, who finds it harder to stop when Max has 3 friends, only hitting counts, and keeping it secret when a friend says telling makes it worse. Each is tested by the task in the same step and the done line quotes the child's guess.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating questions with tagged wrong answers (once, where, hit, words, back, secret, watch, quit); each tag returns its own correction, e.g. 'Watching and saying nothing is being a bystander. An upstander gets help and is kind.' and 'Keep telling. If one grown-up does not stop it, tell another one until it stops.'

readability.evidence: Kid explanation scores FK 1.6 against the family limit of 5.0 using short sentences like 'Bullying is never your fault.' Adult text scores FK 8.3 against 10 and still uses the precise terms: intentional, power imbalance, physical, verbal, social or relational, cyberbullying, bystander, upstander, trusted adult, STOP check.

no_filler.evidence: Filler gate passed. Each kid paragraph adds one part of the definition, the four kinds, or a concrete action; each adult paragraph gives curriculum, terms, named mistakes, or what the lab does. Explanation overlap with every other lesson stays under the 12 percent gate, including Prejudice and Supporting a friend.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360x640 in light and dark: the four kind boxes (Physical, Verbal, Social, Cyber with short hints) fit side by side, the card text wraps inside its tile, the see-saw labels Max and Ava stay clear of the pivot, and the bin buttons wrap in two rows below the canvas. A real pointer drag on iPhone 13 dropped a card into the right box.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs: axe found no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in light or dark on desktop and iPhone 13, no console errors. Every drag has a button twin with an aria-label such as 'Put this card in Cyber' and 'Mark the next day the story says', and the canvas aria-label speaks each story, card and result.

sources: Anti-Bullying Alliance: definition of bullying (repetitive, intentional hurting, imbalance of power)
DfE (2019) Relationships Education, RSE and Health Education statutory guidance: Respectful relationships (types of bullying including cyberbullying, bystanders, getting help)
StopBullying.gov (US HHS): What is bullying, types of bullying
